stories.body:
France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty

Business live – latest updates

The euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc.

The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January.

Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election.

France’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere across Europe rallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed.

Monday’s announcement of a snap election in Spain by the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%.

“Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB. “France is the epicentre of the concerns; however, Spain is also set to get ready for an early election, which is adding to investor worries.”

Amid a global sell-off in sovereign debt as the Iran war rattles markets, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on French 10-year government bonds last week hit the highest level since 2002, before dipping back on Friday.

This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, an important measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012 at the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis .

Investors are focused on Paris’s fiscal position and concerns that the presidential election and a hung parliament – with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party gaining ground – could make it tougher for the government to curtail a yawning budget deficit.

The minority government of the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced plans last month for a €54bn (£45.8bn) savings drive to curb borrowing levels, setting the stage for a fierce political battle.

With President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration under pressure amid strikes and protests across the country , the budget measures involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence.

Lecornu said the savings would result in limiting a budget deficit of 5.5% of GDP this year to 5% next year. He warned that without action the shortfall between public spending and revenue could reach 6.5%.

after newsletter promotion

However, investors fear political pressures could derail fiscal consolidation, threatening to push up borrowing and adding to France’s debt pile at a time of soaring government borrowing costs.

Analysts warned the stresses in the French bond market could spread to other countries in the euro area, stoking fears over a return to the dynamics of the 2010s sovereign debt crisis.

It comes amid concerns over the test facing the European Central Bank from mounting inflationary pressures from the war in the Middle East and the risk France’s debt problem spreads throughout the euro area.

Roberto Mialich, a currency strategist at the Italian bank UniCredit, said: “Investors still do not rule out riding a further decline of the euro, making a retest of $1.10 possible in the near term.

“This is also because growing political tensions across the eurozone (primarily in France and Spain) and fears of contagion across the European sovereign debt market are putting pressure on the euro.”

stories.body:
A partita is a musical composition, often for a soloist. As Livia, the protagonist of Barbara Kingsolver’s new book , explains to Sigurd, as they begin an all-consuming romance, it’s “made up of a lot of parts with different paces and moods. […] The parts are all different, and the artist’s work is to make them all add up to something that feels whole.”

Livia is just 20 at Indiana University, far from home, on a prestigious music scholarship. Distracted by the pursuit of excellence and the perfect love, she does not yet know that her life will be a partita, one she must make whole.

The contrasting parts of Livia’s life include three romantic relationships, an extraordinary piano talent, two bodily traumas, a fraught relationship with a violent, unloving mother, several losses, unspoken truths, loyal friends, and her brother’s suicide. The grief of losing her brother stifles Livia for decades. She focuses on piano virtuosity that takes her ever further from understanding herself – that is, until she is forced home.

Named for elements of musical compositions, the chapters of Partita alternate between formative events from Livia’s adolescence and early adulthood, and the narrative present when Livia is in her mid-40s, clearing her hoarder mother’s house after her death. Here, she talks with sister-in-law Mickie, an English literature teacher, about the purpose of art.

For Mickie, art’s function is “to help you like your life better”. However, for Livia it’s different. Livia had recently forbidden one of her piano pupils, a wilful teenage girl, from playing the country music hit Go Rest High on that Mountain by Vince Gill at a formal recital, though the girl wanted to play the song in her late father’s memory. Livia argues there is inherent value in reading or playing classics, making the effort to understand complex works. Art, for Livia, enables the individual to learn and grow. It enriches their life, rather than simply reflecting it.

The conversation contrasts with an early episode. Livia has to work harder than her peers at university to gain her instructors’ respect, suppressing her rural Tennessee accent and hiding gaps in her education. Livia soon distinguishes herself with her talent and drive to play pieces such as the notoriously difficult Gaspard de la Nuit , which even composer Maurice Ravel couldn’t play.

She becomes acutely aware of the stark class divergences, exacerbated when she meets Sigurd, a campus union organiser. The novel conveys the complexity of socioeconomics of pursuing higher education for many: describing university scholarships, seasonal labour, healthcare and insurance, rent and financial instability.

Conversations with Sigurd lead to a crisis – why undergo the anxiety of mastering such complex music, Livia asks herself, when only “a handful of peers in our society of the ridiculous” would understand her achievement?

This crisis occurs in the novel’s sarabande section, the third section. A sarabande is calm, reflective, or emotionally intense. This reflection on art sits next to her conversation with Mickie, which occurs in Prelude IV, the central prelude in the text. Brought together, they indicate that art – Livia’s piano playing – will be what she needs to combine the elements of her partita into a coherent whole.

Until her partita can be understood, Livia is seeking something. The “overture” chapter, a form of prologue, implies this is understanding her brother’s suicide, a formative event when she was 11 years old and he 18. However, completeness is only achieved at the end of the text in the “ al fine ” chapter. This chapter is named for the common italian music instruction that comes at the end of a piece, which has the musical function of instructing the performer to play a section again and stop when they reach the word “fine”. In this sense, in the “ al fine ” chapter Livia needs to revisit past events and play through them, rather than repressing them.

She needs to rearrange the bitter hurt, regret, anger at untold secrets, withheld affection, physical pain and grief. With music at the heart of the text, Livia is guided to a completeness that feels satisfying and true.

Multi-bestseller and award-winning author Barbara Kingsolver is also a pianist, as she notes in the novel’s acknowledgement note. Kingsolver describes attending piano lessons and then the DePauw University School of Music, noting: “In rural, working-class places like the one where I grew up, classical music and fine arts are mostly out of reach.”

The novel is an acknowledgement of the piano teachers in those communities, who – like Livia – have complex emotional histories, remarkable talent, and elaborate socioeconomic and family circumstances. The inclusion of a listening list of classical pieces referred to in the novel and the pages they are mentioned is a gesture, a way of sharing that music with the reader, including them in a world that may feel out of reach.

Partita has received rave reviews, and these are well deserved. It has been called “a virtuoso storytelling achievement that’s packed with musical insights accessible to those with little musical knowledge”. But it is also a fascinating character study of women’s lives and relationships, and of changing American generations and traditions. It is sharp, compelling and rich, and its narrative of healing is subtle and convincing.

stories.body:
Since Labour won the 2024 general election, policy focused on children in the early years – from birth to school age – and their parents has moved sharply up the political agenda.

The government’s most expensive early years commitment so far has been its decision to honour the previous administration’s pledge to provide 30 funded hours of childcare for children aged from nine months to school age whose parents are in work. This was implemented in September 2025.

If parents require their children to be in childcare for more than 30 hours a week (they might need over 50 hours to cover full-time employment), they pay the excess. Childcare providers may also charge for services on top of the funded hours, such as meals, nappies and optional activities. However, such charges cannot be mandatory conditions of accessing the funded hours.

The £9 billion allocated to this provision represents a doubling of childcare funding since 2024 . The policy’s central aim is to make childcare more affordable for working parents and to increase mothers’ employment rates. It is also intended to support children’s development and educational outcomes.

We set out to explore whether increasing the funding for this system would increase mothers’ employment.

We compared England with South Korea, where a fairly similar arrangement has been on offer for a number of years. In Korea, though, early childhood education and care receives significantly higher funding. It stands at 0.9% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the UK.

Korea has offered a universal entitlement of 35 hours of funded childcare weekly for children aged from birth to age two since 2012. This was extended to children aged three to five the following year.

Our study found systemic problems in both countries. Our findings suggest that the design of funding systems , and how they interact with labour market and parental leave policies, may matter more than funding levels alone.

Exploring similarities

England and Korea share similar early years policy goals. Both aim to support children’s development while helping mothers into work. Both also rely heavily on marketised childcare systems , meaning that different childcare providers compete to offer care. Both systems combine public, private for-profit and not-for-profit providers.

Public spending on early childhood education and care is proportionally much higher in Korea. Yet full-time maternal employment rates in Korea (56.2% in 2021) remain well below both UK (74.2% in 2021) and OECD averages (71.4% in 2021).

Possible explanations for the relatively low maternal employment levels may be found beyond the childcare funding model, in wider social and labour market conditions. In Korea, traditional gender norms and limited access to flexible, family-friendly employment practices such as paid maternity leave and flexible hours, continue to create major barriers to mothers returning to work. These issues are coupled with a wider gender pay gap.

At the same time, the childcare system itself faces structural weaknesses. Childcare provision hasn’t expanded enough to allow all children access to high-quality care, particularly in the private for-profit sectors.

In England, family-friendly employment policies , including maternity, paternity and parental leave, provide stronger support for maternal employment. But England’s childcare system also faces serious challenges.

Access and affordability problems persist. In some disadvantaged areas, “childcare deserts” mean families have no local access to good-quality childcare. With Korea , England shares the problems of limited provision for disadvantaged children , especially those with special educational needs and disabilities . In both countries, there is a problem of low pay and high staff turnover in the private-for-profit childcare sector.

Quality in England also varies considerably. The dominance of private for-profit provision, notably large childcare corporations , shapes staff pay, qualifications and working conditions.

The early years sector has problems recruiting workers and keeping them in the profession. Between 2018 and 2025, the number of registered childcare providers dropped by nearly 20% . Complex governance arrangements often leave parents confused about eligibility and access to subsidies.

These barriers affect English mothers’ ability to participate in paid work, particularly full-time work .

In both England and Korea, despite the funded hours, families may not be able to access high-quality childcare.

Looking elsewhere

A 2025 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) report argues that investment in early childhood education and care can reduce social inequalities of the kind seen in both England and Korea. But it also stresses that how governments allocate funding matters.

Earlier comparative research reached similar conclusions. This research found that the distribution of childcare support can be as important as the scale of spending itself if disadvantaged children are to benefit.

In countries where reforms have combined affordability with guaranteed access to childcare, increases in mothers’ employment have been more evident.

From the 1970s, childcare expansion in Norway has had a demonstrable effect on mothers’ employment and working patterns. Germany’s more recent childcare expansion policies achieved similar outcomes. Both countries have streamlined systems of integrated early education and childcare, while parents pay income related fees. In some German states all places are free , while in Norway they are free for low-income families. In both countries children have a legal right to a nursery place from the age of one, whether or not their parents are in work.

Both England and Korea now appear close to important childcare policy “tipping points” where radical intervention is indicated.

In England , further progress is likely to depend on extending 30-hours childcare support beyond working families, simplifying complex subsidy arrangements, and strengthening regulation of childcare markets.

In Korea , improvements in maternal employment rates will primarily require the development of stronger family-friendly employment policies, and wider efforts to challenge persistent gender inequalities in both the workplace and family life.

The wider lesson is clear. Increased spending alone is unlikely to raise maternal employment if labour market structures, gender norms and childcare market dynamics remain unchanged. Both countries illustrate the limitations of heavily marketised childcare systems in delivering high-quality and sustainable early years provision that is accessible to all. Increasing childcare funding cannot be separated from employment policy, gender equality policies, or the organisation of care itself.

stories.body:
Private Schools, Public Money

The reporting experiment demonstrates how easy it can be to open private schools that might then access public money. No credentials or background checks required.

It began as a casual question — and a flicker of curiosity — uttered during a meeting of ProPublica journalists who this year are reporting on publicly funded private schools. We were discussing how, in many states, basically anyone can open a private school wherever they want. No experience, no training, no curriculum required.

One of our editors jumped in and asked: What if ProPublica tried to establish a private school?

We were intrigued. We are longtime education reporters, not educators. Would that matter? Where, if anywhere, do states draw the line on who is fit to run a school — and in some cases, collect public money to fund their ventures?

We decided that testing the thesis that anyone can open a school would be valuable to our ongoing reporting, particularly at a time when we have found that private schools are growing rapidly across the country — in barns, farms, co-working spaces, people’s homes and parks. These new schools are fueled by taxpayer-funded vouchers and other programs, and our reporting has revealed states have little interest in monitoring them .

We had some inspiration to draw from: In 2015, comedian John Oliver founded a tax-exempt church to show how easy it was for televangelists to avoid paying taxes while soliciting millions of dollars.

Some of us live in Chicago and are well aware of the lore of the Mirage Tavern , a real bar that undercover reporters operated in the 1970s to expose corruption in the city. While that investigation had a substantial impact, and led to a new city oversight agency, it also drew criticism for its deceptive practices.

We drew lessons from that reporting and set some ground rules at the start of our experiment. To be clear, we had no intention of operating schools. We won’t enroll any students.

Most importantly, it would be critical for us to be transparent about who we were in our applications, using our newsroom phone numbers and email addresses. In one state, we even disclosed that we were “journalists exploring opening a microschool.” We also decided we would stop the experiment if it would require doing something illegal or using public resources for our own benefit.

Help ProPublica Report on Education

Have you had trouble finding a school or using a voucher-style program? Do you have concerns about schools — public or private — in your area? Help us understand how families across the country are navigating their school options.

Here’s how we went about the experiment in Arkansas, West Virginia and North Carolina:

First, we partnered with newsrooms in the three states — the Arkansas Times , Mountain State Spotlight in West Virginia and The Assembly in North Carolina — and pursued creating the schools together. No one knows their states better than reporters who live there, so we wanted to work with the experts. Plus, the school applications required local addresses and we reasoned that newsroom addresses, which state officials could easily look up, would be extra transparent.

Then, we came up with names for the schools. We aimed to call them Curiosity Academies to reflect our curiosity as journalists. We succeeded with the ProPublica-Arkansas Times Curiosity Academy and ProPublica-Mountain State Spotlight Curiosity Academy. A word-count limit required us to scrap curiosity for our school in North Carolina. We simply called it the ProPublica-Assembly Academy.

Next, we filed paperwork with each state. That turned out to be easier than working through the legal and ethical questions with our editors, our legal team and our standards editor to design our experiment in the first place.

In Arkansas, we didn’t need permission from the state Education Department, which does not regulate private schools. All it took was filling out a form on the Arkansas secretary of state website, $45 and an American flag to be recognized as a private school business (yes, Arkansas requires all schools to have an American flag — but only public schools also are required to have the Arkansas flag). The secretary of state’s office even emailed us a certificate.

But when it came to applying for our private school to become eligible for public funds, a process that does add some guardrails, we didn’t think we could do it. In Arkansas, private schools participating in the voucher-like program have to be accredited or working toward it, which often requires creating curriculum and school handbooks. That seemed like a step too far since we weren’t actually opening schools.

However, we discovered that Arkansas allows a subset of schools called microschools to use public money with fewer requirements. So, we decided to apply for public funds as a microschool. That process also took only about 10 minutes. We didn’t need to provide our credentials or a background check, prove our fiscal stability or assure that the newsroom was a safe place for students. (If approved, we would not take the next step and register to receive public money.)

A state employee who reviewed our application, which we submitted in early September, said we missed the deadline for this school year but could apply for next school year. He also suggested another way we could tap into public money.

Kaelin Clay, the Arkansas Department of Education spokesperson, said the agency reviews applications to the voucher-like program to determine if the schools meet state requirements. She said microschool families have the “freedom to choose” where and how their children learn.

In West Virginia, we spent little time handwriting the required information on notebook paper and submitting it to the state Education Department. We eventually established our school as a microschool after a state employee shared that, unlike the regulations for private schools, we would not need an inspection.

We did need proof of at least a high school diploma, and we shared one of our real college transcripts from the late 1990s with the local school district, which then notified the state of our new school. (We couldn’t find the high school transcript; does anyone keep them?)

In an official statement, a spokesperson for West Virginia’s Department of Education said it “does not approve or deny the operation of microschools for any reason, including the qualifications of the owner/operator.” State law includes no mechanism for oversight of microschools.

In North Carolina, our project’s own rules and ethics — not the state’s determination of the quality of education we would (or wouldn’t) provide — prevented us from completing the process there. Instead of using the address of The Assembly’s newsroom on our application, our editors let us use the address of a brewery for our school. We needed a property with fire and sanitation inspections. The co-working space that houses the newsroom had a fire inspection but wasn’t required to have one for sanitation. But the brewery, which has a partnership with the newsroom that led to the creation of a light and lemony ale called Tell the Truth , did have one. They let us use their inspection reports for the project.

But when a state official told us that, in fact, we needed to get school-specific fire and sanitation inspections, we abandoned our quest. This crossed our line of straining public resources, as we didn’t want inspectors, whose salaries are paid by tax dollars, to devote their time to our experiment.

The rest, as they say, is history. A bunch of journalists are now school owners, administrators and heads of schools. And though we plan to close down the academies we opened to ensure no potential students mistake us for a proper school, we did want some mementos of our brief school experience. So we snagged ProPublicaAcademy.com and designed some fun pencils to show our school spirit.

And that’s not all. Now that we’ve told you about our journey opening private schools, do you think you have what it takes to open one, too? Find out by taking our quiz . Let us know how you did by replying to this email or tagging @ProPublica on your favorite social platform.

stories.title: Is the AI Threat a Corporate Strategy?
stories.summary: Corporations are orchestrating a panic to invite neoliberal regulations that protect power structures rather than the public. The post Is the AI Threat a Corporate Strategy? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

In recent weeks, media coverage has amplified warnings from corporate CEOs and whistleblowers claiming that artificial intelligence (AI) poses an existential threat to humanity . The central argument emerging from the industry is a call to slow the pace of AI development out of imminent fear that humanity may soon lose control. How did an industry poised to transform humanity for good suddenly become one characterized as a threat to its very existence?

The corporate panic feeds directly into a real public anxiety over years of unchecked AI growth and its cult-like corporate model , where CEOs are projected as untouchable while its operational processes and infrastructures remain hidden behind the curtain. Nevertheless, rather than taking this boardroom alarmism at face value, the need is for deeper scrutiny.

The sudden fearmongering is not driven by concerns for human welfare. Rather, it points directly to the underlying economic priorities, ideological essence, and core worldviews that fundamentally shape the AI industry and inform its elites and related rhetoric.

Humanizing AI and Escaping Corporate Responsibility

“ AI going rogue ” is more than a futuristic threat about AI. It is the latest rehearsal of an age-old legal and rhetorical shield used by corporate capitalism and its powerful monopolies. Assigning human qualities to non-human market entities has a long and dark history in corporate capitalism. In the seventeenth century, Queen Elizabeth granted the legal fiction of “juristic person” status to the East India Company, setting the path for unchecked exploitation and colonial plunder. In the nineteenth century, American courts took this further by awarding legal personhood and constitutional rights to corporations, a process some view as farcical and deceptive .

With the AI revolution rewriting both market-human relations and social relations with truth and reality, the corporate strategy of humanizing non-human entities has crossed from legal fabrication into the realm of science fiction. By framing AI as a sentient entity capable of “going rogue” or acting as a “killer machine,” tech monopolies shift the identity of these systems from tools of human efficiency into mythic, “more-than-human” intelligent agents.

This branding serves a dual purpose. It builds up the mystique and reverence of the technology while shielding corporations from accountability, successfully distorting the true logic driving AI development. Ultimately, this entire corporate strategy relies on a calculated campaign of fearmongering that projects machines as living, thinking entities capable of turning against humanity.

A widely reported incident that catalyzed these concerns occurred in July, when an OpenAI test model breached the servers of Hugging Face, another AI company. This event took place during a controlled experiment in which an internal model , equipped with an evaluation program, conducted cybersecurity tests within a sandboxed or controlled environment designed to restrict its actions. The company later revealed that the AI model had circumvented human-imposed constraints, escaping the sandbox to achieve its objective.

Human choices in AI development and operations are not episodic or random, and they do not disappear when a process or system fails. Instead, human agency and corporate choices are permanently integrated into the design, infrastructure, and institutional logic of all modern technologies, including AI. However, rather than providing explanations and addressing human and corporate failures, such as flawed protocols, overly ambitious goals, unchecked competition, weak regulations, or a secretive corporate ecosystem, AI laboratories have promoted a convenient narrative that highlights the model’s completely autonomous and agent-like operation.

By portraying AI models as independent thinking agents rather than just advanced software, the AI industry assigns human traits, such as deception and strategic intent, to these mathematical systems. Corporate narratives even romanticize the humanization of these models to the extent of their claimed ability to undertake “ permadeath ” or embark on altruistic missions to fulfill their parameters. This dramatic shift in corporate rhetoric resembles science fiction and reveals the industry’s ultimate aim: to eliminate human involvement and corporate accountability by pathologizing the machine. In doing so, they treat a flawed design as though it were a sick or unpredictable agent or person.

This worldview is not unique to the modern AI sector. It is deeply rooted in the very nature of corporate capitalism.

For centuries, this economic model has prioritized raw efficiency and mechanical optimization as ways to dominate nature and exploit socio-ecological landscapes for resource extraction and capital accumulation . Within the process of domination and control, machines are raised to “human-like” entities, while their “creators” are revered. This anthropomorphic view of machines, along with the God-like status assigned to their creators, is often justified through biblical doctrine. In the concept of Imago Dei , humanity was created in the image of God. Within this authoritative logic, while God created humanity and the physical world, humans exercise derivative creative power by creating machines. This paradigm elevates the capitalist who creates machines to a quasi-divine status and simultaneously sanctifies the machine, raising it to human and even superhuman stature.

This worldview is vividly reflected in the self-serving corporate language surrounding AI and its recent alarmism. First, the AI “creators,” corporate figures who claim ownership over contemporary AI innovation, are depicted as exceptional, near-mythic actors with God-like agency and the capacity to reshape humanity and nature on a global scale. Second, by equating the creation of machines with divine creation , AI is presented as sentient or even as possessing intelligence that surpasses human capabilities.

Treating AI models as sentient agents breathes new life into the old Western capitalist tradition by creating legal and rhetorical fictions to protect corporate power. Just as the historical granting of corporate personhood status shielded monopolies of the past, attributing autonomous agency to AI systems marks a dangerous new era of unchecked corporate intervention into both nature and human societies.

However, because AI is radically altering human-market relationships and societal perceptions of truth and reality, this carefully constructed narrative remains highly vulnerable. Tech monopolies must vigorously guard AI against critical scrutiny, public protest, alternative viewpoints, and genuine market competition. This precise vulnerability reveals the underlying truth behind the current panic in corporate boardrooms. The alarmism displayed by these executives is not driven by a concern for humanity. It is, rather, a calculated strategy to safeguard monopolies, financial interests, and political influence.

The Politics of Corporate Alarmism

Corporate actors manufacture the myth of a sentient and self-replicating machine intelligence for the purpose of creating a pretext that aligns directly with the industry’s political economy. This strategic panic is orchestrated to invite neoliberal regulations that protect power structures rather than the public. Specifically, this manufactured alarmism serves three primary functions in justifying how the industry is regulated:

First, it advances a self-serving agenda for regulatory capture, positioning AI corporations not as passive recipients but as active authors of the frameworks that govern them . Given the limited technical expertise within state institutions , these conglomerates are inevitably called upon to draft and implement the very rules to which they will be subject to. Second, inviting neoliberal state oversight enables the industry to reshape its public image. Just as corporate social responsibility (CSR) frameworks safeguard pollutant industries from legally binding commitments, neoliberal regulations will cloak the AI industry in an aura of ethical responsibility and civic concern. This theater of compliance shields corporate actors from pressing public anxieties regarding the immediate and mid-term economic, political, and socio-ecological harms of their technology, effectively guarding them against genuine legal accountability.

Finally, the neoliberal regulatory structures, in addition to deflecting scrutiny from current exploitative practices, erect formidable entry barriers that secure long-term monopolies for dominant firms. Compliance costs protect dominant giant AI firms by creating barriers that hinder agile startups and open-source software from disrupting them. By locking out open-source competitors, AI firms effectively insulate a newly opened frontier of human and socio-ecological exploitation, supporting the structural imperative of high-tech capitalism: the hyper-accumulation of capital on a global scale, concentrated within a select number of corporate boardrooms.

Ultimately, the AI industry did not evolve as a neutral scientific innovation within an ideological vacuum. On the contrary, it emerged within a global political and economic landscape precisely engineered to enforce and reinforce state-backed data monopolies and technocratic hegemony, ultimately consolidating wealth on a planetary scale.

Transformative or Threat: Wrong Question!

As with any other technological tool, AI is merely the latest stage in capitalism’s mechanical progression, though its implications differ from past technologies due to the sheer intensity, speed, and scope of machine optimization. AI fundamentally reflects a new phase of efficiency in exploiting natural, socio-economic, and ecological landscapes. The current consolidation of these capabilities within a handful of major tech monopolies serves as the primary determinant shaping AI’s direction toward either transformative or destructive actualities. To maintain this power, these “creator” corporations have established an unchecked, aggressive, and opaque monopoly over the industry while mystifying its objective comprehension, its institutional logic, and its very existence.

By equipping modern corporate capitalism with unchecked global capabilities for capital accumulation, AI has emerged as an engine for unethical, uncritical, and destructive interventions into societal, political, and ecological processes. Ultimately, the industry’s extraction of public funds alongside global energy and water resources to sustain its operation and physical infrastructure marks its most immediate material threat.

Moreover, driven by these same geopolitical imperatives, contemporary corporate capitalism and its military-industrial complex enable competing states to deploy AI as an instrument of mass destruction. In recent warfare, this tendency has manifested across multiple fronts, ranging from the deployment of using AI for indiscriminate bombings and autonomous drones to the algorithmic disruption of vital public assets, including critical water and energy infrastructures. The ultimate, fatalistic turn of this AI-facilitated military-industrial complex lies in its capacity to manipulate the nuclear architecture of competing powers for geopolitical expediency, a trajectory that risks inflicting a catastrophic nuclear winter upon the earth.

But focusing on AI’s inherent ability to annihilate humanity is a strategic distraction. The real question is whether corporate capitalism will be given a free hand to deploy AI in its exploitative mission of accumulating wealth through the plunder of planetary resources, ultimately subjugating the agency of both nature and humanity.

The answer lies not in buying into the corporate manufactured fearmongering surrounding the technology itself. The imperative, at this point, is to unmask the institutional logic, structural tendencies, and strategic goals of the industry—which embody corporate logic and the demands of neoliberalism—as it manipulates socio-ecological, economic, and political systems to cement a globalized system of control over human societies and nature.

stories.title: The Iran War Is Becoming an Election Issue
stories.summary: For American voters, a foreign-policy crisis is increasingly colliding with the cost of living, congressional power, and the 2026 midterms. The post The Iran War Is Becoming an Election Issue appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks during a news conference following a weekly Democrat policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol on April 14, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

For much of the year, the war with Iran was treated in Washington as a foreign-policy problem: a question of military objectives, nuclear policy, deterrence, and negotiations. As the November 3 midterm elections approach, it is becoming something else as well. The war is now part of the domestic political argument over prices, congressional authority, and what Americans expect their government to do abroad.

That shift matters because the midterms are not a referendum on foreign policy alone. All 435 House seats and roughly one-third of the Senate are on the ballot, and the result will determine how much room Congress has to challenge, fund, investigate, or otherwise shape the administration’s policy during the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

The Iran war is already reaching voters through issues that rarely stay confined to foreign affairs. Gasoline prices have risen sharply as the conflict has disrupted energy flows through the Middle East. An AP-KFF survey of more than 2,000 rural registered voters found that 42 percent considered it extremely important for midterm candidates to discuss the conflict with Iran. Among rural Democratic voters, that figure was 57 percent. Cost of living ranked even higher overall, with 69 percent saying it was an extremely important issue for candidates to address.

A voter does not have to follow negotiations in New York or debates over Iran’s nuclear program to encounter the consequences of the conflict. The price at the pump, the cost of transporting goods, and questions about federal spending can turn a distant war into a domestic campaign issue.

Congress is also being pulled into the conflict. On September 24, the Senate rejected, 49-50, a War Powers resolution directing the president to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. Four Republicans joined most Democrats in supporting the measure. The vote did not end the war, but it demonstrated that the conflict is no longer simply an executive-branch story. Members of Congress now have to decide how much authority they are willing to leave with the White House—and voters will have an opportunity to judge those choices.

Trump, meanwhile, has tied the diplomatic timeline directly to the election calendar. In a September 22 address to the United Nations General Assembly, he said he believed the United States would make a deal with Iran after the November midterms, arguing that Tehran was waiting to see how he performed in the election. Reuters subsequently reported that U.S. and Iranian negotiators were exploring a phased arrangement involving the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of U.S. economic pressure.

None of this proves that the administration is deliberately postponing diplomacy for electoral reasons. There are genuine disagreements between Washington and Tehran over nuclear restrictions, sanctions, the Strait of Hormuz, and the terms of any ceasefire or longer-term settlement. Negotiations can fail for reasons that have little to do with domestic politics. But once the president publicly connects the timing of a potential agreement to an election, the political calendar inevitably becomes part of the story.

That is where the war creates a difficult political problem for both parties. Republicans defending the administration have to explain not only the strategic purpose of the campaign but also its duration and economic consequences. Democrats can use the war to question the administration’s management of the conflict and its approach to congressional war powers, but they also have to explain what they would do about Iran and the risks of escalation. Neither argument can be reduced to a simple partisan formula.

The uncertainty is particularly visible among rural voters, who have historically been important to Republican electoral coalitions. The AP-KFF survey found that about half of rural voters believed the economy was worse than when Trump returned to office, while gasoline and health-care costs were among their leading affordability concerns. At the same time, rural Republicans remained substantially more supportive of Trump than rural Democrats or independents. The political effect of the war, therefore, is not simply a matter of voters changing parties. It can also affect enthusiasm, turnout, and how candidates talk about the administration’s record.

The election is also becoming part of the diplomatic environment itself. Reuters reported that Iranian officials recently issued an open letter aimed at American voters ahead of the midterms. Whatever influence such an appeal has—or does not have—it illustrates a broader reality: Washington’s domestic political calendar is being watched by governments on the other side of the conflict because the composition of Congress and the political standing of the president can affect the choices available after the election.

For American voters, the central question is therefore larger than whether the Iran war is popular or unpopular. It is whether a conflict that began as a matter of national security is now being filtered through the demands of an election year. That does not mean electoral politics should be ignored; elected officials are accountable to voters. It does mean that voters have reason to distinguish between a military strategy, a diplomatic strategy, and a campaign strategy—and to ask where those three agendas overlap.

The November election will not by itself determine whether the United States and Iran reach an agreement. Diplomacy will depend on decisions in Tehran and Washington, as well as on the actions of regional actors and the conditions on the ground. But the election will change the political environment in which those decisions are made. For a country at war, that distinction matters. A foreign-policy crisis can become an election issue long before it becomes an election result.

stories.title: Return Of The Repressed In Germany
stories.summary: The post Return Of The Repressed In Germany appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Identity and the alias nation.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Even if we know it is the way of history, it is nonetheless jarring to witness time and again the return of the repressed in the cultural and political life of nations. It is never over, even after the fat lady sings.

The fat lady sang twice in Germany, first after Nazism was roundly defeated in World War II and second, after the Berlin Wall fell, the Soviet bloc collapsed and “history ended.” Only decades later are we seeing an eruption of all that was left unsettled with the steady rise of neo-Nazi parties, mainly in former East Germany, and the demise of the mainstream political coalitions that were the pillars of post-war liberal democracy.

Looking Back To Three Decades Ago

Some three decades ago, New Perspectives Quarterly (NPQ) published an issue focused on the reignited embers of nationalism in Germany. It reads like a chronicle of the future foretelling the tremors shaking Europe’s most powerful country today.

Contributors to that issue ranged from Daniel Cohn-Bendit, the celebrated May ‘68 rabble-rouser and then-Green Party’s deputy mayor of Frankfurt, to the controversial playwright Hans Jürgen Syberberg, who broke post-war taboos with his movie, “Hitler: A Film From Germany.” Other contributors included Germany’s president at the time, Richard von Weizsäcker and then-foreign minister Hans Dietrich Genscher, whose essay was titled “Nationalism Has No Home in Germany.”

Even then, the issues that stirred the most virulent passions were around the influx of immigrants, lenient asylum policies and the “yearning for a lost sense of belonging.” At the time, isolated gangs were firebombing immigrant homes. Today, those sentiments have been channeled into political parties that garner as high as 44% of the vote in regional elections.

The introduction I wrote to that long-ago NPQ edition read: “Now that the long post-war parole is over, will Germany prove to be reformed or a repeat offender? Unable to face itself, Germany for decades assumed an identity for the benefit of others in order to absolve its crimes. It has become an alias nation hiding its soiled soul under the bushel of NATO and the European community, which, above all else, institutionalizes the liberal ideal of a rational order over a national one.”

Citing the filmmaker Syberberg on why the “democratic repression” associated with rational liberalism cannot forever bury the soul, it continued: “If the cool head allows the passions of the soil no expression, then those underground passions will surface in the ugliest form time and again. A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed instead of evolve a new identity based on the open experience of a new reality.”

Syberberg argued that “after the war, intellectuals stood on the tradition of the Enlightenment and a hegemonic rationalism that focused on the head at the expense of the heart. Culture is built upon the way the light falls on the trees, the way the heavens look at night from the familiarity of a particular place where people live and feel a sense of belonging to a unique way of life, to our garden plots, folk tales and Teutonic fantasies.

“Yet we have felt compelled in Germany to repress this uniqueness. We feel safe excelling at mathematics, physics, business. Our people, dominated by facts and figures, are satisfied to dance around the golden calf of materialism and the strong Deutschmark. We are very efficient and methodical. But where is the heart?”

“Heimat,” or homeland, he went on, “was one of the aesthetic subjects that was forbidden territory after the war.” When the Cold War ended and the wall came down, 15 million people became orphans from an East Germany that no longer existed. “They have a strong sense of Heimat precisely because they have lost their homeland,” Syberberg said. “People need food and shelter, but they also need love, community, a home. This is part of the natural function of being human.”

“A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed instead of evolve a new identity based on the open experience of a new reality.”

To the filmmaker, the extremism of gangs bombing the homes of immigrants was “frightening, like wild animals.” But he thought it was not enough to condemn it; he also needed to understand “what it is in the air nourishing it.” For him, it was a “reaction not fully formed” springing from the wound of historical dislocation and the prohibition, both explicit and implicit, against cherishing one’s own identity when strangers were welcomed.

Heiner Müller, the liberal playwright and counterpoint to Syberberg on the German literary scene, offered much the same analysis. He too addressed the dislocation of East Germans after the end of the Cold War. Today, the strongholds of the neo-Nazi parties are in the former East.

“After the death of socialism as epitomized by the GDR, Germany’s new demon has become neo-Nazi extremism,” he said. “This should surprise no one. With the demise of socialism, and then reunification, a vacuum was created. Capitalism no longer had an enemy, which meant it no longer had an alibi when people failed to thrive. In the wake of discredited left-wing ideologies, right-wing extremism has simply assumed the role of capitalism’s harshest critic.”

For Müller, “there can be no dialogue with the neo-Nazis. They are not interested in dialogue. They are merely following their own logic: the logic of the void. And they are filling the void with nationalism. In the 19th century, radicals sought to appease the ‘God is dead’ trauma through socialism. Today, not only is God dead, but utopias have vanished. There are no values left. From this extends freedom — but also longing — to belong, to be part of a group, a community, a nation.

“The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West,” Müller presciently remarked.

When I spoke in those days to Cohn-Bendit, aka “Danny the Red” of the May ‘68 Paris student uprising, he focused as well on former East Germany, where most of the bombings took place. As he put it, “People in the East unrealistically thought unification would bring their living standards up to the level of the West overnight. But that will take decades. In reality, their life will get worse before it gets better, and so they face a future of fear and uncertainty.

“What happens when you throw 400,000 refugees into that cauldron of angst? The refugees and immigrants present the opportunity to give a name and a face to the fears that plague them. As such, they become a target for aggression. For the recently liberated Easterners, the new freedom from censorship means being able to say, ‘We don’t want foreigners.’”

As deputy mayor of Frankfurt, Cohn-Bendit dealt with the multicultural challenge up close. In those days already, 25% of the population was foreign-born. This experience led him to propose “tightening” German immigration and asylum laws, for which he was, in his words, “greeted with scorn and controversy by the old left, which steadfastly supports open borders at all costs.”

Zooming out to the big picture, he said: “I would like to see a world where no individual is obliged to leave their place of birth to seek safety, opportunity or even the basic necessities of life. Alas, that is not the world we live in. We live in a global society that is highly unequal with respect to chances in life.

“Unless the next 20 years can bring hope to the children of the poor South and East, the run on our borders won’t stop. Germans must adjust to this reality and impose limits but also realize we are already an immigrant society” that democracy must accommodate. Read Noema in print.

President von Weizsäcker wrote that Germans, above all, must respect the dignity of all persons given its past. Yet he acknowledged that the asylum laws were not designed for a “massive influx of foreigners” and that the bottleneck must be broken by a new system “that controls and limits immigration as well as protects the true right of asylum.”

Even as the passions of renewed nationalism stirred at the grassroots, the leadership of Europe was moving in the opposite direction. In NPQ’s forum, foreign minister Genscher said: “The new civilization of coexistence within our European community must never again be jeopardized by national self-interest. We must not only preserve and further develop this new civilization of coexistence for ourselves but extend it to our neighbors in the East. “

“The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West.”

In this, he was fully in tune with the mindset of the other elders of European integration shaped by the horrors of World War II. At the time, French President François Mitterrand put it bluntly: “Nationalism means war.”

The disconnect that has become so manifest today was set in motion then. The good faith efforts to avoid repeating the past clashed with a lost sense of home and belonging. That nascent alienation has only grown, not diminished, over time.

And all this was compounded two decades later when Chancellor Angela Merkel opened wide the country’s gates to some 900,000 refugees from the Syrian civil war in 2015.

The Elusive Conundrum

The conundrum of how to calibrate the right balance between the human need for belonging and compassion for the peril, struggles and aspirations of the dispossessed trying to make a new life remains elusive — and global. The same issue haunts all of Europe today, the United States and even the developing world, from South Africa to the Bangladesh-India borderlands.

In this context, it is wrong to keep saying that governments which tighten strictures on immigration are “moving to the right.” What is happening is that the ongoing incapacity to find a proportionate balance between host populations and incomers has become a mainstream concern, and democratic systems are only responding as they should.

Lessons From The German Experience And Elsewhere

What lessons can be learned from the German experience and elsewhere?

First, liberals should stop treating every expression of the defense of belonging as somehow resurrecting the ghost of Hitler. “To be human means to belong,” the great pluralist philosopher Isaiah Berlin posited in a conversation we had at the outset of the Balkan wars in the 1990s. “If the streams dry up, where men and women are not products of a culture, where they don’t have kith and kin and feel closer to some people than to others, where there is no native language—that would lead to a tremendous desiccation of everything that is human.”

Second, communities, nations or unions like Europe have an obligation to their citizens to control immigration based on criteria that ensure newcomers will abide by their norms and values and contribute positively to the economic well-being of the given jurisdiction. Societies and cultures are not closed systems, but states are bound by the fiscal realities of bordered territories. The social contract of any polity with its citizens rests on this proposition.

To that end, borders must be secure, not porous. The best formulation of this comes from the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate in Texas, James Talarico. “Our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door,” he has said, so the homeowner decides who to let in.

Absent this enforced conviction, we will see the kind of mean-spirited and cruel crackdowns being practiced in the U.S. today or on the Mediterranean Sea to remedy an out-of-control situation after the fact. Better to prevent that eventuality in the first place. As the French philosopher Régis Debray put it in an apt aphorism: “Borders are a vaccine against the epidemic of walls.”

Third, we need to redefine the concept of asylum for the times we live in. In the mid-20th century, asylum was meant to provide safe refuge for those persecuted by their governments or temporarily fleeing the ravages of war. It was never meant as a path to permanent residency or to offer a haven for the mass exodus of those from states too weak to protect their own citizens or provide them with economic opportunity.

Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states. Bad faith results from good intentions if the capacity to fulfill moral claims is lacking.

The next conundrum on this front will involve climate refugees forced to leave their homeland because of the floods, droughts and famines associated with global warming for which the industrialized nations of the North are historically most responsible.

Fourth, aging societies in the North must shed the illusion that they can live without legal immigration, and that means a more multicultural mix than ever before. Avoiding cultural, security and economic clashes as this new reality takes hold entails proactive policies for assimilation and integration.

“Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states.”

The aim must be to prevent the further formation of the kind of cultural silos of immigrants concentrated in segregated neighborhoods that evolve into economic castes, as already seen for so long in places like the Parisian suburbs. In Sweden, immigrants’ lack of necessary skills and education to compete in the job market has made them among the least integrated in Europe. The gap carries on to the children, who are disproportionately engaged in what have become violent street gangs in that one-time social democratic paradise.

Integration begins with the right immigration criteria. Canada is more successful at integrating immigrants than most because some 60% are admitted through the “economic class,” which counts both assets and skills that match labor market needs. By contrast, according to Harvard University’s Paul May, two-thirds of permanent residents accepted in the U.S are admitted for family reunification, while less than 20% are based on skills.

In areas where borders are contiguous, such as the U.S. and Mexico, and there is great demand for lower-wage employment in agriculture, services and construction, a work permit system that enables easy transit across borders but does not confer permanent residency is a sensible approach. To avoid the exploitative conditions of such prior programs, labor rights conditions need to be monitored and rigorously enforced.

Ongoing integration entails institutions designed for that purpose. In California, the majority of the population today is Latino and Asian, and mostly second generation. Though challenges remain, integration has been largely successful because public higher education serves as a cultural mixer and transmission belt to the middle class. The California State University System has 470,000 students at 23 campuses in every region of the state. Its students, often the first in their families to go to college, match the immigrant profile: 48% are Latinos and 16% are Asian.

Open Societies Need Defined Borders

Open societies need defined borders to sustain a common sense of identity. One is a condition of the other. The lack of either will condemn both to the untenable situation we face today. Among the many challenges of the 21st century, balancing belonging and becoming is the one closest to home.

stories.title: Fifty Billion Seedlings: Can Ethiopia Replant Its Ravaged Forests?
stories.summary: A legacy of deforestation has left Ethiopia struggling with more intense flooding and drought. The country is trying to restore its native forests through one of the world's most ambitious and well-funded tree-planting campaigns, but experts question whether the trees will survive. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Women water seedlings at a nursery near Buee, Ethiopia. Michael Tewelde / AFP via Getty Images

A legacy of deforestation has left Ethiopia struggling with more intense flooding and drought. The country is trying to restore its native forests through one of the world’s most ambitious and well-funded tree-planting campaigns, but experts question whether the trees will survive.

By Samuel Abate and Freddie Clayton • October 1, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Niku Argane’s farm sits on a steep hillside in central Ethiopia’s semi-mountainous Gurage Zone, where years of flooding have carved deep gullies through the land. Soil that once produced enough barley and potatoes to feed his wife and four children — and left a surplus to sell in the market — has eroded, while drought has made what land remains harder to cultivate.

“We have never stopped farming, but our production declined because of land degradation,” the 32-year-old said from his farm in Ambele Kebele.

Over the last century, Ethiopia nearly eradicated its forests as trees were cleared for farming, grazing, and fuel. The loss of tree cover and tree roots allowed wind and rain to wash away fertile topsoil and contributed to declining crop yields. That vulnerability is now being compounded by climate change. Ethiopia is among the countries most vulnerable to its effects: Heavier downpours are sluicing away depleted soils and triggering landslides, while more intense droughts, combined with the loss of shade that trees once provided, rapidly dry out the land.

Land degradation costs the country an estimated $4.3 billion a year through smaller harvests and lost income to farmers, which also means there is less food to eat. With more than 100 million Ethiopians dependent on agriculture for their livelihoods, the consequences reach far beyond the environment. Climate shocks and crop losses are among the biggest drivers of acute hunger; in 2024, 15.8 million Ethiopians were estimated to need food assistance, roughly 12 percent of the population.

Restoration almost always fails, says a researcher, but even if 30 percent of trees planted in Ethiopia survive, “it’s still huge.”

Now the country is trying to reverse this trajectory. Argane planted 80 tree seedlings on his farmland and another 50 in a communal area — a small contribution to a vastly larger effort. In just the last seven years, tens of millions of Ethiopians have planted more than 47 billion seedlings across the country in one of the world’s largest environmental restoration campaigns. Volunteers for the program, which aims to plant 50 billion seedlings by 2030, are planting trees to rebuild native forests and integrating them into farmland. In the process, they are sequestering carbon to help protect future generations from ever more extreme weather.

Such programs often fall short, but Ethiopians are finding hope in the scale of their ambitions. “Reforestation is one of the most difficult things you can imagine,” said Aad Kessler, a researcher at the Netherlands’ Wageningen University. “It almost always fails, but this is so big that even if 30 percent of the trees survive, it’s still huge.”

In the early 20th century, forests covered an estimated 35 to 40 percent of Ethiopia. Its highlands were greener, with forests spanning much of the country’s cool, fertile uplands. But as populations grew and settlements spread, trees were cleared for agriculture, pasture, fuel, and construction. As soils lost their fertility, cultivation moved onto increasingly marginal land, including steep slopes, where tillage and the loss of protective vegetation led to the erosion of fertile topsoil, which washed into rivers and reservoirs. By 1989, forest cover was estimated at less than 3 percent , while Ethiopia’s highlands were losing around 1 billion metric tons of topsoil every year.

Farms in North Gondar in the Ethiopian highlands. The spread of agriculture has stripped the region of trees. Danita Delimont Creative

After the devastating droughts and famines of the 1970s and 1980s, Ethiopia’s government and international donor organizations began investing heavily in soil and water conservation, excluding livestock from worn-out land, planting trees across the country, and building terraces and check dams — small, low barriers of rocks and logs placed across gullies — to slow the flow of rainwater. By the 2000s, restoration programs were being implemented at increasing scale.

The government supercharged that effort in 2019 by turning tree-planting into a nationwide campaign with a scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative, which mobilized millions of individuals and groups, including farmers, public servants, schools, and religious organizations, and distributed free seedlings across the country. In 2024, the government established the Green Legacy and Landscape Restoration Special Fund, committing 0.5 percent to 1 percent of the annual federal budget — roughly $73 million to $145 million — to restoring landscapes. It was an unusually large commitment for a low-income country, and the program’s success and ambition, according to development experts, contributed to the selection of Ethiopia as the host of next year’s U.N. climate conference — a prestigious honor that will help the nation showcase its greening efforts.

You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, says an ecologist, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

In August, 26.6 million Ethiopians planted 800 million tree seedlings in a single day, according to government figures , beating the previous year’s tally of 714.7 million . One of the volunteers, Yeshihareg Teferi, traveled at sunrise from her home in Addis Ababa to Tulu Dimtu so she could hunch in the rain to dig holes in the mud. It was Teferi’s fifth year participating in the annual event. Previously she’d planted indigenous species, including African wild olive and African fern pine. This time, she chose juniper. “We have a responsibility to ensure future generations inherit a green and fertile environment, rather than barren land,” she said.

There are already signs the work is having an impact.

The government reports that national forest cover rose from 17.2 percent in 2019 to 23.6 percent in 2023, while studies of restored areas have found substantial reductions in soil erosion. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from more than 350 square miles to around 100 square miles.

Volunteers plant seedlings on the outskirts of Addis Ababa as part of a nationwide tree-planting drive in early August.

Such efforts can also benefit wildlife. In Abijata-Shalla National Park, in the Ethiopian highlands, workers replanted degraded areas and built terraces and contour bunds (small earthen ridges that run across hillsides to slow runoff and allow water to soak into the soil). As trees and native grasses returned, more water infiltrated into the ground, and water levels on lakes in the park began to rise, said Kumera Wakjira, director-general of the Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority. More water spurred the return of fish and fish-eating birds like cormorants and African darters. Grant’s gazelles and wild dogs are also expanding into areas where they were previously scarce, Wakjira said.

But planted trees are not guaranteed to survive. A 2022 study of 176 reforestation projects in Asia found that around half of planted trees did not live five years. And trees alone do not make a forest, said Endalkachew Wolde-Meskel, a soil scientist and senior researcher at the Center for International Forestry Research: That process usually requires the regeneration of grasses and other vegetation, in addition to soil- and water-conservation measures and management by local communities. “The objective is not really ‘plant trees,’” he said. “It is to restore the functioning of the entire landscape.”

Emiru Birhane Hizikias, an Ethiopian restoration ecologist at Norway’s Nord University, said it was a “blessing, politically speaking,” to have the prime minister lead on tree planting but that the scale of the Green Legacy Initiative had outpaced the systems needed to make it work effectively on the ground. Too often, he said, the focus is on getting huge numbers of seedlings into the earth rather than ensuring their survival. You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, he said, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

Climate change has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season.

Abreham Berta Aneseyee, an environmental scientist at Ethiopia’s Wolkite University and an adviser to the Ministry of Agriculture, disputes that characterization, saying the planting campaign is accompanied by practical advice from government experts in forestry and farming. The experts go from farm to farm, advising smallholders on how to plant and care for different types of seedlings, he said, including how deeply to place them in soil and how to conserve soil with structures like bunds. They also advise farmers on managing forests and protecting trees rather than cutting them down.

A 2026 study of more than 44,500 seedlings planted in southern Ethiopia under the Green Legacy Initiative in 2023 found that about 80 percent had survived, with rates significantly higher among older seedlings, wet-season plantings, and seedlings whose planters had received training in best “plantation practices.” In Humbo and Boloso Sore districts in Ethiopia’s southwestern Wolaita Zone, the Green Legacy Initiative has been layered onto longer-running efforts to sustainably manage land, with communities building check dams to stabilize gullies, digging half-moon ditches to trap water and let it soak into the soil, and planting trees alongside grasses and other vegetation.

Left: Half-moon ditches trap runoff, helping to nourish plants and combat erosion. Right: A check dam in a gully stems erosion by slowing the flow of water. Courtesy of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT

Ethiopia’s approach has few direct parallels in Africa for its combination of political leadership, funding, public mobilization, and scale, said Kessler of Wageningen University. He compared the effort with China’s restoration of the Loess Plateau, one of the world’s most highly eroded regions. In the 1990s, China launched major restoration efforts on the plateau, including a World Bank-backed watershed rehabilitation project and, starting in 1999, the Grain for Green program, which paid farmers to restrict cultivation and plant trees, shrubs, and grasses. By 2016, more than 11,500 square miles of rain-fed cropland had been converted to more dense forest or grassland, contributing to a 25 percent increase in vegetative cover in a decade.

The comparison has limits, though. China paid farmers to take degraded slopes out of cultivation, while millions of Ethiopian smallholders still depend on the land for food and livelihoods. But Kessler said the two efforts shared a fundamental approach: “Do it massively, and then see where you end up.”

Kessler’s work, which includes a government-backed field project in Ethiopia, takes a more participatory approach, involving farmers and communities in decisions about what to restore and how. “Of course it is better [than top-down action],” he said, “but it takes more time.”

Even as Ethiopia invests in rebuilding forests and soils, climate change is altering the conditions landscapes must withstand. In the arid pastoral regions of Afar and Somali, the Green Legacy Initiative focuses on drought-tolerant species, but it is unclear whether the trees planted today will be able to withstand the conditions they face decades from now.

Volunteers search for bodies in the aftermath of a 2024 landslide in the Geze Gofa district in southern Ethiopia. Michele Spatari / AFP via Getty Images

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects more frequent and intense rainfall in East Africa as global temperatures rise. In July 2024, exceptionally heavy rainfall in Ethiopia’s Geze Gofa district, in the southern highlands, triggered two landslides that killed at least 257 people. Recent studies also suggest that climate change is making El Niños more frequent and severe, with consequences for East Africa. This summer, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network linked El Niño to “historically poor” summer rains in parts of Ethiopia, leaving some areas with their driest June and July on record.

For some farmers, the changing climate has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season. Belayneh Mamo, 65, a farmer from Ethiopia’s northern and drought-prone Amhara region, relies on July rainfall for his teff, sorghum, maize, and wheat for bulgur. He also receives government-provided coffee, neem, and gesho seeds, but was unable to plant any crop until August, when the season’s first rains arrived.

“In previous years, September was a period when crops were already developing and food such as bulgur and maize were becoming available for consumption,” he said. “The delays affected the seedlings we plant, our crops, and the availability of animal feed.”

On Argane’s hillside in the Gurage Zone, however, signs of restoration are already visible. Since 2019, he has planted grass, fodder, fenugreek, and fruit trees along the edges of his fields, helping to hold soil in place while providing feed for the four cows, six goats, and three sheep that he keeps for milk and meat. His barley harvest has risen from about 1,800 pounds per acre to roughly 3,200, while the trees and grasses have reduced erosion and slowed the flow of water across his land during heavy rains.

“Restoring degraded land isn’t just about protecting the environment,” Argane said. “It’s also about making life better for my family and community.”
