Justice secretary vows courts backlog will reduce

Published 4 October 2026

The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.

Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much.

He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making".

The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.

Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns.

Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst-case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035.

There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused.

Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape.

Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences than that would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing the right of defendants to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of being cleared.

The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.

'Swifter justice'

Norris earlier said that he remained committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice.

But he added: "I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course.

"This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.

"Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment. I remain committed to structural reform which is crucial if we are to bring down the backlog."

Old Bailey: All Crown Courts hear trials by jury

Andrew Thomas KC - chairman of the Criminal Bar Association, which represents barristers who work in crown and magistrates courts - said the profession was "delighted".

"Justice needs juries," he said. "Nothing inspires more public trust than 12 ordinary citizens from all walks of life deciding the facts of a case together.

"We are also pleased that the government is going ahead with important changes in the bill to protect victims and witnesses at trial. These include new powers to prevent unfair questioning about a complainant's behaviour and to support witnesses to give their best evidence."

But Thomas warned plans to keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates could backfire - not least because of a shortage of magistrates.

"The proposal to strip defendants of their right to elect a crown court trial, combined with doubling magistrates' sentencing powers to two years, would shift 25,000 cases a year - including 5,500 jury trials - out of the crown court," he said.

"These are not minor offences. It includes serious and sensitive cases including assaults, sexual assaults, child abuse and grievous bodily harm. Our volunteer magistrates do an excellent job but they are completely unequipped to try complex, multi-day trials.

"It would be a car crash if they tried to do it, especially at this time."

Claire Waxman, victims' commissioner for England and Wales, said victims were "being asked to place their faith in a plan that ministers themselves argued would not be [enough]".

Barrister Karl Turner, a Labour MP who was suspended from the parliamentary party after he criticised the government's plans to reform jury trials, thanked Burnham "for his support during my campaign".

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour have been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the Crown Court."

Liberal Democrat justice spokeswoman Jess Brown-Fully added the proposal "should never have been introduced in the first place", while Green MP Sian Berry said it was "a victory for justice and fairness".

Watch: Daughter of Sir David Amess says MPs are no safer today

Published 4 October 2026

The daughter of murdered MP Sir David Amess says politicians are still at risk and questioned if anything has changed five years after her father's death.

Katie Amess told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg what happened to her father "wasn't an isolated incident, we are seeing increased threats towards members of parliament".

Sir David was the Conservative MP for Southend West when he was stabbed multiple times while holding a constituency surgery in Leigh-on-Sea, Essex, in October 2021.

The government commissioned a review into his death in August , to identify lessons to be learned and recommend steps to minimise the risk of future tragedies.

Katie Amess, pictured earlier this year, has long campaigned for a public inquiry into her father's murder

The review is being led by former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland, with the aim of reporting within six months.

The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years since the death of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe in July this year, Sir David's murder in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox's murder in 2016.

The five years since her father was killed have been "absolutely devastating and heartbreaking", his daughter told Kuenssberg, adding: "It's a very, very real situation that we're living with."

She has previously called for a public inquiry into the safety of politicians so people can have "the full facts to hand, full openness, honesty, and transparency".

The nearing anniversary of Sir David's murder comes after the man accused of murdering Widdecombe was also charged with preparing acts of terror, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Amess, who knew Widdecombe as a family friend and called her Aunt Ann, said: "It's absolutely so tragic and heartbreaking that now she isn't here either."

She added: "My dad was murdered five years ago so if so much has changed why are we still seeing other members of parliament or former members of parliament being targeted like this."

Widdecombe was not a sitting member of parliament when she died, but was a member of the Conservative Party and the member for Maidstone and the Weald from 1987 to 2010. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.

Sir David Amess was stabbed to death at a constituency surgery on 15 October 2021

Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.

Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29.

"I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".

Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be".

"We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."

Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."

She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.

His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.

A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

Watch: People shouldn't be punished for working harder, Badenoch says

Published 3 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch has said a Conservative government would scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, the Conservative Party leader said: "What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so."

The earnings limit means only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for 30 hours of government-funded childcare or tax-free childcare.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch, who arrived in the city on Saturday, has vowed the party was new and different from the one that lost the 2024 general election.

The Conservatives - who have been polling behind Labour and Reform UK over the past year - are expected to use the four-day event to lay out more of their policy agenda ahead of the next general election.

Ahead of the conference, the Conservatives produced a 100-page essay setting out their principles , external including a "central" belief that business, rather than governments, create growth.

It argues that governments should create the conditions for growth, particularly through the tax system.

In her interview with the BBC, Badenoch pitched herself as a "classic old-school Conservative" adding: "I believe in common sense - people working hard and being rewarded for that effort."

She insisted the Tories would keep the state pension triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to change if Labour wins the next election.

She said the policy, under which state pensions rise each year by the highest of inflation, average wages, or 2.5%, was "the right policy for pensioners".

She added: "What we don't want to see is people going after the elderly, chasing after vulnerable and disabled people, and then the extremely large cohort of people who can work, who are not working, are left alone."

The Conservatives have long called on the government to cut the growing welfare budget including by implementing tighter restrictions on claimants.

'Wrong choices'

The party said its childcare announcement would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare , external for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year, although all three and four-year-olds are eligible for 15 hours of free childcare, regardless of parental income.

The same £100,000 eligibility threshold also applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme , external , and has remained unchanged since it was originally set under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government.

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power, they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely for tax-free childcare and government-funded childcare hours.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

In her interview with Kuenssberg, Badenoch said: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1m a year getting free childcare under a Conservative government, the Tory leader responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

What does childcare cost and how do government-funded hours work in England? Published 21 May

Education secretary to ask competition watchdog to review hidden childcare costs Published 25 May

Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference Published 3 days ago

The Tories argue the threshold may mean some people may delay having children until their incomes change, or decide not to start a family at all, describing scrapping it as "both pro-family and pro-growth".

By providing an increased incentive to work, the Tories said the move would also boost economic growth.

They added that it would tackle the "unfairness" that the threshold is calculated on an individual earner's income rather then for the whole household.

The party said the policy would be funded by cutting the number of public servants working in "executive non-departmental public bodies" - organisations which have a role in the processes of national government but operate at arm's length from ministers, such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

It said this would save £1.6bn by 2029-30, covering the estimated £700m cost of removing the childcare "cliff edge".

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Decision by Paramount Skydance executive David Ellison was relief to employees who feared overhaul – and possibility of Bari Weiss taking over

Mark Thompson, who since 2023 has served as chair and chief executive of CNN after a storied career in British and American media, will retain his role even after Paramount Skydance takes control of the company, he announced in a memo to network staffers on Monday morning.

While Thompson wrote that the “specifics of how CNN will plug into and operate in the new company have yet to be finalized”, he offered some pledges about his role at the combined company, which will be led by David Ellison, the Paramount Skydance chief executive, after the company merges with CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery. The deal is expected to formally close on Tuesday.

“First, I’m convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company,” Thompson wrote. “They’ve seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are.

“And second, having now spoken to them at length on the topic, I have real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for. That’s why I will be leading CNN into this new chapter as it becomes one of Skydance’s suite of major media assets and global brands, and leading it as an independent editor-in-chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now.”

The decision by Paramount Skydance leadership will bring relief to many CNN employees who feared a complete overhaul of the network. Some employees had also shared concerns that Ellison could install Bari Weiss, editor in chief of CBS News, atop the cable news network. (The Wall Street Journal first reported that Ellison had asked Thompson to stay on.)

“That sound you hear is a giant sigh of relief from halls of Techwood,” said a CNN producer, who was not authorized to comment, referring to the company’s Atlanta headquarters. That sentiment was shared by other CNN employees who spoke with the Guardian.

According to an announcement of the combined company’s leadership team, Weiss will also remain in her role as editor in chief of CBS News, despite some speculation about a potential change in her purview.

Thompson, 69, was brought on to take charge of CNN in 2023 after the tumultuous leadership of chief executive Chris Licht, who lacked network management experience and lasted just over a year. Thompson had previously served as director-general of the BBC from 2004 to 2012 and then as president and CEO of the New York Times from 2012 to 2020.

At CNN, Thompson has prioritized the network’s digital and streaming operations, as well as the creation of a new direct-to-consumer product called CNN All Access in October 2025. The CNN producer credited Thompson with “stabilizing” the business and helping to build its post-linear television future.

Thompson has also had his hands full with Donald Trump’s White House, which last month barred CNN – along with MS Now and Politico – from the building before a judge temporarily restored access.

A former longtime CNN producer said that Thompson’s presence would be reassuring because he is a known entity. “They know what he brings,” the person said.

When Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery closes on Tuesday, after the settlement of lawsuits aimed at blocking the deal, the company will begin the process of integrating the various media assets it has acquired.

It is unclear if, when or how CNN and CBS News will be merged, though they will share a parent company. The two networks have different corporate structures and serve different audiences. At an industry conference on 30 September, Paramount’s chief legal officer, Makan Delrahim, noted those distinctions. “CBS News is a handful of hours of programming,” he reportedly said . “CNN is 24-7. Just completely different markets.”

While both CBS News and CNN have large American audiences, CNN has a much larger international footprint, and there has been speculation that its foreign team could take precedence if the companies are merged. There is also the expectation of widespread layoffs across the entire company, including at CBS News and CNN, as part of an effort to slash costs.

And there have been concerns about whether the Ellison family, which controls a large chunk of American media and entertainment assets, could move CNN in a more conservative direction, a fear that Ellison himself has dismissed.

As part of a settlement reached between Paramount and a coalition of 12 state attorneys general last month who sued to block the deal, the company has agreed to create a five-person news editorial independence board within 180 days of closing the deal. The board will “establish guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels” and will ensure those principles are adhered to. But some employees at CNN and CBS News have dismissed the planned board, fearing it will lack teeth.

Thompson hinted at the uncertainty surrounding the merger in his memo. “I know many of you have had trepidations about this moment. That’s understandable – indeed, as I’ve hinted before, I’ve had the odd moment or two myself!” he said. “But I want to say that on the eve of the acquisition of CNN by Paramount Skydance, I find myself in a very positive frame of mind. I really do believe we’ll be working alongside a team who don’t just have real vision and real energy, but real values as well.”

Thompson told CNN employees that he would have more details to share on Tuesday.

Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
stories.summary: It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei

Published 51 minutes ago

The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.

The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement.

Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August.

But multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.

It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.

A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.

It is not clear why the defence department has stopped using the company's tools now. The details of the department cutting ties entirely have not been previously reported.

Anthropic had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.

But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI tools.

When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.

Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.

Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules Published 28 August

Anthropic sues US government for calling it a risk Published 9 March

Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons Published 11 September

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down Published 12 September

As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI.

OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department

The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.

It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.

Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.

Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system.

"The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said.

"Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official.

Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White House

The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.

Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran.

Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.

Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.

'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI

Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage.

The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.

Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.

Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration.

Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week.

After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI.

"How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".

Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

stories.title: BT agrees rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk
stories.summary: The takeover still needs to be approved by the regulator, but would give certainty to TalkTalk's millions of customers
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 October 2026, 07:37 BST

The UK's biggest broadband provider, BT, has agreed to buy rival operator TalkTalk to save the company from collapse .

The takeover would end of months of speculation over the future of TalkTalk and mean services for its millions of customers will continue as normal.

BT boss Alison Kirkby said it provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers. The administrator, Alvarez & Marsal, said it also provided certainty for TalkTalk's 900 staff based in Salford, Greater Manchester.

However, Virgin Media called it a "stitch-up" which allows BT to "tighten its grip" over the market. The government has given itself the power to have the final say on the deal, citing its importance to vital public services.

TalkTalk has 1.5 million retail customers and one million wholesale customers across the UK.

BT's Kirkby told the BBC's Today programme: "Two and a half million customers, including vulnerable households, and key emergency services might have lost their services if Talk Talk had failed, which it was on track to do.

"So BT stepped in as we were the only viable option to take the business forward."

Ernest Doku from comparison website Uswitch said the deal means "nothing changes today".

"Your broadband and landline carry on as normal, and there is nothing you need to do right now," he added.

However, he said that BT should explain "quickly and plainly what this means for contracts, prices and service in the future, so nobody is left guessing".

The regulator, Ofcom, says broadband customers should have the right to leave a contract without an exit fee , external if a new owner puts the price up beyond what was in the contract.

TalkTalk began as a challenger to BT in the broadband market. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange, but was taken over by private equity in 2021.

Since then, the firm has built up debt while losing customers, leaving it unable to pay some of those it owes money to.

Despite this, TalkTalk remained the fourth biggest broadband provider in the UK, with 6.6% of customers, during the March to June period of this year, according to figures from analytic firm Opensignal.

BT has 32.5% of customers, Sky 19.9%, and Virgin Media 19.1%.

Rivals who were beaten to the deal by BT have said it will be bad for consumers.

Tom O'Hagan, a former TalkTalk executive who was leading a takeover bid for the firm, told the BBC he was worried about "reduced choice and potentially an increase in price for consumers and for businesses" because of the BT deal.

He added that he was particularly concerned about competition in the wholesale market, where TalkTalk's subsidiary PXC was BT's main rival.

Virgin Media, which has also reportedly tried to buy TalkTalk in the past, said the BT takeover has "all the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest".

It added that the purchase means BT can "roll its tanks over competition and further tighten its grip on the market. The logic simply doesn't add up."

The Competition Markets Authority (CMA) will need to approve the takeover, which would give BT greater power over the broadband market.

Tom Smith, a competition lawyer and former legal director at the CMA, said the regulator will be balancing that concern with other considerations.

"When the CMA looks at it, it will look at what would have happened if the deal wasn't going through," he told the BBC.

"If TalkTalk would have exited the market, for example, then really any deal is better than TalkTalk exiting, but then there might be alternative bidders as well that would have been less anticompetitive."

However, the Department of Culture, Media, and Sport (DCMS) has given itself the power to make the final decision on the deal in the name of the public interest once the CMA has made its report.

DCMS has given the CMA until 19 October to deliver its verdict.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure.

"If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including to hospitals, schools and emergency care. These are unprecedented circumstances that require action now."

BT has said it welcomed the intervention and would "work constructively with the government and the CMA during their review".

Judith Mackenzie, a partner at investment manager Downing, told the BBC that broadband was "not a regulated industry, unlike electricity and water, but it's also very important to business users and ourselves, consumers".

"It's almost like a commodity now, broadband," she added.

BT has said it will cost the firm £400m to buy TalkTalk out of administration.

This includes the purchase price, fees, TalkTalk's expected £60m loss for this year, and BT effectively writing off the £100m TalkTalk owes BT's Openreach business.

TalkTalk has £1.5bn of debt and made a £100m loss last year.

stories.title: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?
stories.summary: At least 23 huge data centres are planned in Scotland, causing significant concern for campaigners.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A Google Data Centre in Cheshunt in Hertfordshire

Published 7 hours ago

Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes.

Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale.

The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world.

Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres.

Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs.

Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make.

So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles?

What is a data centre?

The data centre proposed at Chapelcross would be one of the biggest in the world if it went ahead

From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse.

On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI.

While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering.

Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense.

One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife .

The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches.

What's the controversy?

There have been a number of protests against data centres

AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves.

At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie , which has a capacity for 12MW.

The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level.

If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.

At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village.

Other concerns focus on:

their size and impact on the landscape

the amount of electricity they require

the water needed to cool equipment

noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems

The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.

The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium.

Why build them in Scotland?

One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector.

Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed.

However, experts caution that this does not mean data centres would run entirely on renewable energy .

During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking.

Don't data centres use a lot of water?

The scene inside a Meta data centre in Temple, Texas.

As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating.

While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain.

An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead.

And what about the hum?

Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife.

What are the potential benefits of data centres?

Many of the proposed data centres are in Scotland's central belt - including an expansion of the company DataVita's site in North Lanarkshire

As well as having a stake in a key future technology, those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs.

Lanarkshire has been designated an AI growth zone by the UK government, with data centres at its heart.

When it was announced in January , external , £8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs were promised.

The type of jobs a data centre creates has also been debated.

About 800 are expected to be in AI, with 50 apprenticeships. The rest are in construction.

Apatura - the developer behind 10 of the hyperscale data centre proposals in Scotland - highlights its green credentials with its access to renewable energy and battery storage.

What are the politics behind it?

With China and the US hoping to win the AI race, the UK government does not want to be left behind.

The Scottish government also supports the investment in the AI growth zone.

In August, it announced that ministers would have to be notified of proposed centres over 50MW in capacity.

A month later, it rejected the Scottish Greens' call for applications to be paused until new national guidelines are in force.

However, it said environmental impact assessments would have to be submitted.

The government also said it was "highly unlikely" any large data centres would be given the green light before Christmas, and promised that new guidance would be published by the festive season.

stories.summary: A new play about the art-loving Bloomsbury Group member speaks of the enduring battle of ideas with his free-market rival Friedrich Hayek The sound of guns from the advancing German armies could be heard clearly by John Maynard Keynes as his train trundled across northern France in the spring of 1918. The evidence of the struggle on the western front was everywhere but Keynes, then a Treasury official, was not heading to Paris on war business; he was off to buy some art. Keynes made the risky trip to attend an auction of the studio of Edgar Degas, who had died the previous year. The man who would become the foremost economist of the 20th century returned to London with some impressionist treasures for the National Gallery, having successfully petitioned the chancellor of the exchequer to spend £20,000 at the sale. The production, which will have a short run of 30 performances, is to feature new routines as well as his famous sketches from TV shows including Not the Nine O’Clock News. “It is 40 years since I last did a comedy sketch show in the West End,” said Atkinson. “I thought it would be fun to perform again the sketches that began it all for myself and [writer] Richard Curtis, and in which my most well-known characters originated, alongside some surprise new material written especially for this show.” He and Curtis will be collaborating once more with Blackadder writer Ben Elton and its composer Howard Goodall.
